utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, everyone. Today is the 26th of March, 2007. As you've noticed the President, Patrick Robinson, Judge Patrick Robinson is not with us today, and I will be the acting Presiding Judge. Under Rule 15 bis of the Rules, the Trial Chamber believes that it can sit; and on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I would like to greet everyone in this courtroom, starting with the representatives of the OTP, with Mr. Whiting and his associates. I would like to greet the Defence with Mr. Tapuskovic, his co-counsel, and his case manager. I would like to great the accused, General Dragomir Milosevic, the registrar, and all personnel assisting the Trial Chamber. With regard to the Defence, the Trial Chamber has learned that Mr. Tapuskovic has lost someone very dear to him, and the Trial Chamber would like to express its deepest condolences to him and hope that he has found necessary strength to continue working in these proceedings. In this Tribunal we work according to the principle of the publicity of the proceedings. The public will have noticed that the Trial Chamber did not sit last week; and for the record and to inform those who watch the proceedings, I would like to state that the Trial Chamber was not on vacation. The Trial Chamber went on site together with all the parties, and I would like to thank all the parties who took part. I would like to thank the Office of the Prosecutor as well as the Defence for the spirit of cooperation they've shown throughout our stay in Sarajevo. This is what I wanted to say. We are now going to resume the regular proceedings with a witness today who has just taken the solemn declaration; and according to the Rules of Procedure and is evidence, I would like to make sure that the witness can understand me in his own language. If that's the case, please say that it is the case, Witness. Please say that you understand. Witness, do you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to ask the Prosecutor to tell us what sort of witness we're dealing with today. Is this is a viva voce witness or is this a 92 ter witness we have in front of us? And what is your time estimate? How much time will you need for the examination-in-chief? Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. And on behalf of the Prosecution, our condolences also to Mr. Tapuskovic for his loss. To respond to Your Honour, this is a viva voce witness. I have been allowed two hours for the direct examination, and I will do my best to finish it in less time than that, if possible, but I may have to take the full two hours. I note that we -- I won't be starting till about 12 or 13 minutes past the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So please go ahead, and keep in mind that the 27th of April is the date by which the Prosecution is supposed to finish the presentation of its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. We have in mind, Your Honour, though, that topic will be the subject of a motion from the Prosecution, which will be received shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Luka Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Colonel, in order to save time and unless there is an objection, I am going to summarize your background, and then just ask you to confirm it when I am finished. So if you could please listen carefully to what I say. You were born on the 14th of November, 1951. You graduated from the Air Force Military Technical Academy in Rajlovac in 1972, and you were then a member of the JNA. In 1992, you were a lieutenant-colonel in the air force academy in Rajlovac and still an anybody of the JNA, the army of the former Yugoslavia. You became a member of the VRS, the army of the Republika Srpska, on the 19th of July, 1992, and on that date you were appointed Chief of Staff of an infantry brigade in Visegrad. That infantry brigade was first known as the Visegrad Brigade, later known as the 2nd Light Infantry Podrinjska Brigade. When the Drina Corps was formed in November of 1992, that brigade part of the Drina Corps. You were appointed commander of that brigade on the 26th of October, 1992, and you remained commander until August of 1993. At that time you were appointed head of a staff of the Visegrad Tactical Group to coordinate the work of various brigades. Is that all correct up to now?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Then at the end of November or beginning of December 1994, you were appointed as an assistant commander to General Dragomir Milosevic who was then the commander of the SRK, and you were the assistant commander in charge of morale, religion, and legal issues, and you had the rank of colonel. You held that position until the end of the war sometime in 1996. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, just a few questions about how you got here today. Were you interviewed by the OTP in August of -- of 2006?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of August, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for the precision. After you were interviewed by the OTP, were you contacted by the Defence in this case, and did you agree to be a witness for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: After that interview, I was told that a month later an investigator would give me a call and ask me if I was willing to testify for the accused; however, that didn't happen. Three -- more than three months elapsed when he called me and asked me again if I wanted to be a witness for the Prosecution if I required any protective measures. In the meantime, Mr. Milosevic's wife called me by phone and asked if I wished to be a witness for the Defence. I told her what I already said a minute ago. I described the situation with the OTP investigators, and this month that he had indicated had already gone. I told her that if the Defence believed that I should testify, then I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just to summarize, the answer to the question is, yes, you agreed to be a witness for the Defence at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I would give testimony if necessary both for the Prosecution and the Defence, and I stand by that statement. In my mind, it is only logical that as an assistant commander for morale to be on the side of the Defence; that is, to give to evidence on behalf of my commander. It's only normal, given that I was his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just one final question on this topic before we move on. Were you subpoenaed here to testify today? Did you receive a subpoena?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the next topic, which is the laws and regulations that applied in the army of the Republika Srpska. And just so you're aware, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, my questions to you, sir, are going to be on very narrow and specific topics. They're not going to be wide-ranging. You will see they are going on very specific purposes. The first topic is on laws and regulations. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what -- what was the relationship, if any, between the rules and regulations that applied in the JNA and those that later applied in the VRS. Just generally and briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Initially, the rules of the JNA were applicable on the VRS. Later on, these rules were amended but the basis were the rules of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 1654, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, these are regulations from the JNA from 1988 on the application of international laws of war in the Armed Forces of the SFRY. Did these rules continue to apply when the VRS was formed in May of 1992 and when you were a member of the VRS? Did these rules continue to apply?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P474, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we now look please at 65 ter exhibit 1692, and if we could zoom in on the lower right of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Colonel, this is an order on the application of the rules of international laws of war in the army of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's dated 13th of June, 1992. I want to draw your attention to paragraph 2, which we have to go to the next page of the B/C/S to get to paragraph 2. It's on this page of the English. It states that commanders and commanding officers and each member of the army or other armed formation shall be responsible for the application of the rules of international laws of war; and then it goes on to say: "The competent, superior officer shall initiate proceedings for sanctions as provided by the law against individuals who violate the international laws of war." Was this an order in place during the entire time that you were a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was this consistent with your understanding of the obligation of commanders to initiate proceedings in the event of a violation of the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question was perhaps unclear. Was this -- in this provision, paragraph 2, it states that superior officers shall initiate proceedings in the event of a violation of the laws of war. Is that consistent with your understanding of the obligation of a commander in the VRS during the time that you were a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, could you please inform us who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page -- if we scroll down on English, it may be visible. Yes. It's issued by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to bring this into the terms of the SRK, just to be clear, under this provision, under this order, and specifically paragraph 2, if a brigade commander in the SRK or the corps commander of the SRK became aware of a violation of the international laws of war, did he have an obligation to report that to the military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: His duty was to initiate proceedings and -- through expert organs in the command, and send an appropriate document to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in the event that a brigade commander took this step; that is, initiated proceedings, did he have a duty or obligation to report that to the corps command, up the chain, and report that he had done that to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, in regular reports, this information was included as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move to another topic, and that is to focus in --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar, can we have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P475, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to another topic and focus on the time that you were the assistant commander in the SRK for morale, religion, and legal issues from the beginning of December 1994 until sometime in 1996. When you were in that position, did you receive information from the military prosecutor in Sarajevo about cases that had -- criminal cases that had been initiated?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The corps command, or rather, its legal department received such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the legal department, just to be clear, was it under our your command; that is, did it fall under your command?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of responsibility, in the military parlance that would be subordination. However, according to their professional competence, they were responsible to superior command levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how often would you receive this information from the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: The military prosecutor's office had their schedule of work, and supplied this information to the corps command most often once a month. So you may say it that it was a rule, and this applied to the previous month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In other words, they would supply the information in -- in one -- in one month, and it would be about the month that had just completed, the previous month?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the next month for the previous month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In addition to sending the information to the corps command of the SRK, would the Sarajevo military prosecutor send the information to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose they did, but that's the purview of the military prosecutor's office, so I don't have exact information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let ask me the question more directly. Would he send it to -- was there a -- in addition to there being a Sarajevo military prosecutor, was there a military prosecutor above him for the entire VRS?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And would the Sarajevo military prosecutor provide the monthly information also to his superior, the VRS military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a superior to the Sarajevo military prosecutor, but my assumption is that he must have relayed the same information to a higher level through his chain of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you received the information from the Sarajevo military prosecutor, what would you do with it, if anything?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: We would inform -- inform members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command during regular briefing sessions; and then in an appropriate form, it would be conveyed to lower levels of command; that is, brigade command in order to inform both the officers and soldiers in the brigade. The essence of this information would be the same as the one received from the military prosecutor. However, it wasn't so much elaborate, only examples of behaviour were provided to lower level. So each individual case is being listed in this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look please at 65 ter number 2397. I'm going to look now at some examples of this reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this is a report that is dated the 2nd of June, 1995, and it is from the military prosecutor of Sarajevo, Todor Todorovic. And it is to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, specifically to the organ for morale, religion, and legal affairs, and it is information about the crime trends in the month of May 1995. Do you recognise this document; that is, is this the type of document that you would receive from the military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P476, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just before we move to this document, take note that this document is dated the 2nd of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now if with we could look at 65 ter 2410, and could we go to the second page in English, please. I'm sorry, I meant the second page in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a document which is dated the 6th of June, so four days later, and this cover page is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could have the English on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The cover page is from the military prosecutor of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that's not the right English page. That's it. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Supcic, and it is entitled, "Report on crime trends in May 1995, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now if we could turn to the second page of the document, or let's say the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Attached to this document is the document that we just saw from the 2nd of June, 1995, from Todor Todorovic. Is this consistent with your understanding of how the military prosecutor of Sarajevo would send the report to the VRS military prosecutor, and then the military Prosecutor of the VRS would put a cover page on it.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I assume; that this is the way that it was, but I do not have direct knowledge as to the way in which Prosecutor's offices functioned at different levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go back to the previous page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Based on your dealing with these sorts of documents at the time and your familiarity with the VRS, and just -- paying attention, looking at the format, the stamp, and the signature of the document, does this appear authentic to you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, here I cannot see the stamp. But apart from that, I think that this is the way things usually were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, can we have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P377, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Whiting, sometimes I do not respond immediately because I'm waiting for the interpreter from the French booth to finish translating so that explains why I take sometime to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't mean to rush, but I do mean to rush. If we could look at 65 ter 2416, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is now a document which is dated two days later, the 8th of June. So the first document was the 2nd of June, 1995 from the Sarajevo prosecutor, then the 6th of June from the VRS prosecutor attaching the same information. This is now the 8th of June, 1995. Do you recognise this document, sir? And perhaps we will have to be turn to the next page for you to be able to see the signature page. Would you like to see the signature page?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the page?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go to the first page now of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: This is information that the legal department of the corps command sent to lower ranking commands, or rather, legal officers in brigade commands, with a view to informing officers and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically -- sorry to interrupt. Specifically, this was sent to the forward command post of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Just --

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I can explain what a forward command post is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: That is part --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have actually had evidence on that, but I appreciate it. Can you explain what is the relationship of this document to the document we saw just a moment ago that was from the Sarajevo military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the basic source for compiling this kind of information, or rather, the information that is right in front of us is the preceding document that was received from the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now if we could go to the last page of the document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does the last page, in the left there on the bottom, does it indicate to -- to whom this information, this report was sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Scroll down on the English to the bottom there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Colonel, does it say who this was -- to whom this was sent?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says to all units. Specifically, this example that you're showing here is what was sent to the forward command post where part of the officers from the corps command were and part of the soldiers from the command who are supposed to provide security and everything else that is required for the forward command post to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P378, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, we've just looked at the three reports from the Sarajevo military prosecutor, then the cover page put on by the VRS military prosecutor, and then, finally, your report summarizing the report of the Sarajevo military prosecutor. These were all written in June for the month of May, consistent what you had explained to us. Now, what I would like to do is go through each month to show you reports, similar reports for each month. Unless -- if the Defence would accept into evidence all of the reports for the months that have been disclosed, I could save time and not go through it; otherwise, I will go through each month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are absolutely in accord. All those reports that exist from the month of September all the way into 1995, we agree that they be admitted into evidence. I don't think there is any need for repeating all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could I then just -- if I could just provide the numbers, the 65 ter numbers and then they could be given exhibit numbers, and I will tell you what months they're for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Whiting, in principle, we are not against what you're suggesting. We've taken note of the fact that the Defence agrees for all these exhibits to be tendered into evidence. However, we would not like to be flooded under documents that might not all be relevant. These exhibits you would like to tender, are they all relevant for the case here in these proceedings and for the indictment in these proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour. And there are only ten documents. It's one or two for each month, and they are all within the indictment period and they're all relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, if we look at the document we have here in front of us, we are talking about disciplinary measures taken in relation to violations of the rules that apparently at first site have absolutely no connection with our case, with our indictment. Therefore, I'm afraid I would not like to be flooded under documents of that kind; but if you give us the assurance that all the documents, all the exhibits you want to tender are relevant to the indictment, then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I give you that assurance, and I could explain why that particular document is highly relevant, but I'd rather not take the time now to do that. For December 1994, the report is 65 ter number 2200; for February of 1995, it's 65 ter number 2259; for March of 1995, it's 65 ter 2311 and 2313; for April of 1995, it's 65 ter 2336; for June of 1995, it's 65 ter 2522 and 65 ter 2554; July 1995 is 65 ter 2567; August 1995 is 2628; and October 1996, it's 65 ter 2678. If those all could be given numbers at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 2200 becomes exhibit 479; 65 ter 2259 becomes exhibit 480; 2311 becomes exhibit 481; 2313 becomes exhibit 482; 2336 becomes exhibit 483; 2522 becomes exhibit 484; 2554 becomes exhibit 485; 2567 becomes exhibit 486; 2628 becomes exhibit 487, and 2678 becomes exhibit 488.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I want to move on to a new topic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the time-- during the time that you were assistant commander for morale, religion, and legal affairs from the beginning of December 1994 until the end of the war, do you recall any instances where a commander from the SRK reported a criminal violation of the international laws of war to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I never learned of or heard of something like that happening in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in the period that you refer to. As far as I can remember, if there had been any such thing in these reports from the Prosecutor's office, then certainly officers from the command would have received information about that and appropriate measures would have been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you explained to us before about how reporting occurred within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So if there had been a report made by a commander from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps about a violation of the international laws of war, would you have known about it and would the corps commander have known about it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I would have to know about it, or rather, that officer, well, depending on his level, in daily combat reports, inter alia, there would be information of that kind, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to another topic which is to look at some additional reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 2174, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Whiting, just a brief question to the witness. Witness, you state that the according to your information no member of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was ever prosecuted for war crimes or violations of the Geneva Conventions or for any violation of humanitarian law by the Prosecutor of Sarajevo. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated that I never received such information, nor did I personally learn of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could look at the document on the screen, this is a document dated the 27th of December, 1994. Was this signed by you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 2318, please. This is a document that's dated -- an order that's dated the 22nd of April, 1995, and if we could scroll down to the bottom. It's the bottom of the B/C/S that I'm interested in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You signed it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you explain how that occurred, because it has the name of Dragomir Milosevic, but you say you signed it. How did that occur?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is subject matter from my own line of work, the commander gave me approval, consent as his assistant commander that I could sign such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear, did he approve this particular --

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean to interrupt you. Let me just ask this question. When you say he gave you a approval, did he approve this particular document, or do you mean he gave you approval generally to sign documents under his name?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: No, only from the purview of the work of the organ that I headed. As for this specifically, he probably gave me instructions and authorised me to sign it. The document was created by the legal officer in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at the first page of the document. It's already on the first page in B/C/S, but the first page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the subject heading is, or rather, the two line says "to be delivered to," and then it says "PRB commander." What does PRB stand for?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment please. Well, since I didn't see this, let me say something. As this is an order, for every order I had to get specific approval that from the commander that I sign it on his behalf. I as assistant commander did not have the right to command. As for this abbreviation, I think that it is Pracanski Battalion. The Pracanski Battalion. That is the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was the Pracanski Battalion a battalion within the SRK?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: It was. Although, I do not see here who exactly who this was submitted to. I cannot see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the -- I think you have the entire document before you, so ...

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have the letter P, but that doesn't really mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I understand. Just to be clear, in other words, what you're saying, and correct me if I'm wrong, is that you don't know who received this, whether it was actually received?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I was saying. Over here, I cannot see exactly who this was submitted to. I cannot see it on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, on the line that says --

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: This is a reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But on the line it says "to be delivered to," and then it says "PRB commander." What do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I have already told you, but I really cannot see it here. Where is that written?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. If can he could zoom in on that, it is at the top of the document. I didn't understand that it was hard to see. Do you see that now?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I think it is the Pracanski Battalion that was within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That battalion had written to the corps command with regard to certain problems. They asked for an opinion, and by way of an order we regulated this; that is to say, how this problem should be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P490, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look now at 65 ter 2546. This is a document which is dated the 18th of June, 1995. We still don't have the English. There we go, and if we could go down to the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that your name at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My first and last names are typed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, do you -- looking at this document and maybe we have to scroll to the top, do you know how this document was prepared?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted by my assistant for legal affairs, a lawyer. This is a dispatch. It is not a classical written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was your assistant for legal affairs authorised to write this dispatch. Did he receive authorisation to do that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This particular line of work is directly related to morale. Since I was not in the corps command, it was done by the professional who was in a position to do that on my behalf. I was out in the field, and I agree with everything that people who were under -- that was done by people who were under my command. This is a team that worked in harmony and with responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, registrar, please, do your job.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P491, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I note that I took just 50 minutes to complete the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Congratulations. As we still have 30 minutes, I'm now turning to the Defence. I don't think there are any questions for the moment. Mr. Tapuskovic, if you'd like to begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I thank the trial and you, Judge Mindua, the President and my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, for their expression of condolences. However, let's me begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, I'm Defence counsel for Dragomir Milosevic. As you know, it is true and you may confirm that if you know that at the time while you were not yet on the Prosecutor's list of witnesses, through my investigator in Sarajevo I tried to get in touch with you as well as with any other commander. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask you something about Dragomir Milosevic who was your immediate superior officer. I'm not going to suggest anything to you. I would simply like to ask you to tell us, if you can, in the briefest possible terms, and I'm kindly asking you to make the best of the time allocated for this cross-examination, I would appreciate if you could give me brief answers, probably yes or no. However, with regard to this question, I would like to ask you to tell me in your own words something Dragomir Milosevic, about a commander, a soldier and a person. Can you tell us briefly, tell the Chamber briefly about that.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was a professional of the highest ranking. He was an a extraordinary personality. He knew that a victory cannot be achieved in the office but rather in the field. I can say that 90 percent of his time is spent in the field with lower ranking units, brigades up to the lowest ranking unit that is a platoon. In view of the operational position of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, he needed enormous time and energy in order to accomplish these tasks. I would like to underline that he was a man of high moral values. He was an altruist, and never did I hear from him using the word enemy for the opponent. He never considered any people his enemy, both in official capacity and when we went together to inspect the units. I never heard anything like that from him. He was an exceptional professional and a person of high moral values.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know and can you confirm that he was a fiercest opponent to the use of alcohol and that he imposed the most stringent measures on all soldiers using alcohol in the field?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was fiercely opposed to that and to a large extent he was successful in implementing this first and foremost by setting an example himself and he managed to put this into practice. I cannot say for sure whether it was up to the lowest level but as far as he was able to keep this under control he was fully successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And he pronounced short imprisonment measures for people who were found intoxicated?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, either directly or he issued an appropriate order to his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, in line with good customs applicable by the Serbs he always kept a bottle of homemade brandy in his office which he served to his visitors?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And it was customary for him, as far as I know, he would just toast his guests especially if those were VIPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move to specific topics and I'm kindly asking you again to give me the briefest possible answers in order for us to conduct and finalise this dialogue in the Chamber for the benefit of what needs to be down. Can you confirm that, since you said he was such a professional, honoured and abided by the decisions of the General Staff and that he never took any decisions that went outside the lines that were set up by the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also confirm that all of decisions that you know of were always in the spirit of the general decisions take by the Supreme Command and the General Staff and also that they were fully in accordance with international law?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Given that I said that he was highest professional is self-explanatory and the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When he dealt with civilian authorities, can you say that he primarily contacted them with regard to the basic needs of the army, the food, the fuel, the humanitarian aid? In other words, the provision of basic necessities for an army to sustain?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that he never succumbed to any political or civilian pressures in any way whatsoever, Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a short while ago I checked with the colleague of Mr. Whiting whether there's -- whether there's a translation of document 0529411, and our number is DD00-1903. There's only a B/C/S version of it, and today I'm very seldom going to use B/C/S documents. I have documents that have been translated. I would like just to put a few things to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now you can see this document. It's dated 9th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me, no. It was signed by the head of the legal department, by my authority. He was a superior of mine -- correction subordinate of mine. My name has been typed out by I authorised him to sign this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1 briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the first sentence which reads as follows: "Recently attempts by the municipal and higher authorities -- leadership of the SDS, that is the Serb democratic party, to infiltrate in any possible way and excerpt influence on a command and control." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, let's look at that. It says: "Basically attempts are being made to discredit the current commanders and to have them replaced and to bring in their place SDS officials." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, is it fair to say that various political intrigues often threatened to undermine the reputation of various commanders, and here I primarily refer to Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was second nature of civilians, that they liked to interfere with military affairs which is something that the least know about. The commander wouldn't allow such practices, and the undermining of the command and control by the civilians structures. He reacted whenever he heard of any such instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I feel somewhat blind because I have the B/C/S text on my screen. But in this particular case, I want to make sure that what you have just read out tallies with what the interpreters of the Tribunal have up on their screen. I'd like to check this with the OTP to make sure that the content is what we have here. Is that right, Prosecutor, because we don't have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, I'm as blind as you are. I -- I don't have a translation either, so I'm unable to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, do the interpreters have this text on their screens.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They should be able to see the B/C/S channel in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do I have to read again what's already been confirmed by the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I had and opportunity, Witness, just to listen to the audio recording of your statement. To this date, I haven't received it in writing this interview, except in English. I don't have a B/C/S version of it. However, after listening to this interview, I remember and I know that the OTP showed you a document from November which is the time when you were not discharging your duties in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Do you remember that there was mention about some meeting with civilian authorities? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I saw it in this document, but I heard about that for the first time in this interview with the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You had no direct knowledge about this issue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you were deeply convinced that it must have been only a kind of intrigue when political and civilian authorities interfered with military affairs with a view to discrediting certain officers, and here I refer primarily to Dragomir Milosevic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document marked for identification and be given an MFI number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D135.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I proceed with my questions to this witness, Colonel Dragicevic, I have in my hands a very short document on his appointment dated 22nd November 1994, number DD00-1891. It's a very short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now on the screen, Colonel Dragicevic. It's dated 22nd November 1994, and it was signed by Commander Dragomir Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: His name is typed out, but I don't know whose signature this is. This letter was drafted by someone with the initials SK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate --

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: But this is the document issued by the SRC command?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is authentic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So someone else signed on behalf of Dragomir Milosevic within the authority given to this person by Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This could have only be signed by personnel officer, and he had power and authority to do that for this specific kind of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it reads: "The above named shall be charged duties of the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's no mention here of being in charge of legal affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But in military terms and in terms of the setting up of this department, I was superior to the legal department in its functioning as a military formation, not in professional and expertise because I'm not a lawyer, and I cannot be a superior to a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, that is what I wished to clarify before the Trial Chamber. You had a military education, and you did not have any kind of training as a lawyer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We just had what any professional officer has by way of completing the Military Academy or higher ranking levels of education. It is only natural to act in accordance with the rules, but in essence that does not mean that we have training as lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you had lawyers who had degrees in law who worked on documents for you and, of course, after that you would sign these documents or you would authorise somebody else to sign these documents? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That is to say, experts in particular fields, educated trained people, who had their training verified, they are the ones who created professional documents. And those who had the right to sign documents and to put a seal, a stamp on it, did so, especially when given authority by the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. I have a question to put to the witness. You were heading, I believe, the legal department or part of the legal department of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that right? So below you, you had lawyers or I believe these must have been officers that belonged to a totally different department, totally different from the military magistrates; by that, I mean the military prosecutor of Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. We did not have any connections in terms of superior or subordinate levels in terms of subordination with the military prosecutor. The military prosecutor in Sarajevo did cover the same zone as the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; however, the corps command had nothing to do with the military prosecutor's office in terms of subordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But in your particular department, you had a number of officers that had -- were trained lawyers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain this for you. In the organ for moral, religious affairs, and legal affairs, there was a department for legal matters. There is was a department for morale that I headed, and at the same time I was assistant commander. And according to establishment, there was a department for religious affairs. There was a trained lawyer with a degree in law in the legal department and also a person with some legal training at post-secondary level and also a person who was a typist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honour, Judge Mindua. I did wish to deal with the matter, but you have done so already. That is why I would like to ask for this document,, DD00-1891, be admitted into evidence, or rather, marked for identification until it is translated. It is a very brief document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, could you please enlighten the Chamber a bit and tell us what the document that you seek to have admitted really is? What is the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, this is a document appointing Colonel Dragicevic assistant commander for morale, religion, and legal affairs in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the 22nd of November, 1994. This document shows when he assumed this duty, and when he became department commander. So this a document that related to his appointment, and his appointment to this duty precisely on the 22nd of November, 1994. That is when he came to this position, and from that moment, of course, he bears certain consequences as commander in the sense that is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, the Trial Chamber, of course, would have liked to admit your document but we have no translation, so we can just marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Mindua that is precisely what my proposal was, that it be admitted but just marked for identification. It is very brief, but I haven't tendered it until it is translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you give us a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D136.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If could you please give me answers that are as brief as possible to these few questions before the break. You can confirm, can you not, that in the beginning of August 1995, Commander Dragomir Milosevic went to Belgrade for medical treatment due to an eye injury that he sustained in a situation at the front line.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that we had great difficulty in talking him into doing that; although, the medical complication was already quite serious. The wounding took place a couple of months before that. So in spite of all of that, he barely agreed to do that, or perhaps it would be better to put it this way. We had great difficulty in talking him into this; that is to say, to have this resolved so he could continue his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also confirm that as for this medical treatment in Belgrade in hospital, and then treatment at home, he stayed all the way up to the 10th of September until the NATO air-strikes began against the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that he cut his sick-leave short, and he came to the command post; that is to say, to the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just another thing, if you could give me a brief answer: Did he spent most of his time at forward posts at the Nisic plateau, which is up in the north, and then at Trnovsko, or rather, the Trnovsko part of that front in trenches most of the time, rather than in Lukavica where the command post was? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as I have already said in the beginning, I think, was a commander who knew -- who won battles and where. He knew that battles were won by well-motivated soldiers with a high morale and high discipline. That is why I'm sure that he spent over 90 per cent of his time, at least while I was there when I could see this for myself, he spent out in the field due to the position that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had. For example, in order to visit a brigade in Ilidza, the command corps was away from the commander of the Ilidza Brigade, only five or six kilometres as the crow flies. In order to get there, you would have travel for three or four hours in the summer, and during the winter about five hours along roads that were under possible constant fire by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, we're going to stop now. It is now 32 minutes past 10.00, and we will resume at 50 minutes to, 20 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragicevic, now I would like to deal with a subject as quickly as possible, so could you please give me the briefest possible answers. At the moment when the conflict started in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, can you tell me where you were exactly?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, or rather, in Rajlovac, at the air technical centre, that is where I was serving.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Although you were there in terms of your duties, you did nevertheless receive information about what was going on in the country, right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were informed along the military lines, or rather, it was compulsory to inform all officers, or rather, all members of the Yugoslav People's Army about what was going on in the country. This was done by way of the media as well. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am sorry. I am just wondering if we could clarification about when -- what time-period we're talking about here, because the reference is to when the conflict began, but that can mean different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, you've heard the question put to you by Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand this full well, and I can spell it out in more specific terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know full well what it was that was going on late in June 1991 in the territory of the Republic of Slovenia. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By way of our information and through the media, I know what was happening there. That is how I was informed. That is how I learned about things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in first and for most and what should be explained to the Trial Chamber is the following: This army, the Yugoslav People's Army, up until those days that I referred to very specifically now, the Yugoslav People's Army was deployed like any other country, in the territory of the entire country. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, it was in Slovenia, in Croatia, in Macedonia, in Montenegro, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in Serbia, of course?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the barracks; and for the most part during a period of 45 years, it carried out peacetime duties only, putting out forest fires, building roads, railways, only peacetime tasks, and assignments. Do you know about that as an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, it carried out training, which is what its purpose was anyway; that is to say, training people to protect the country, to defend the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information through military channels or through the media that the Territorial Defence in Slovenia had attacked the Yugoslav People's Army? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn that between the 25th and the 27th of June, the Territorial Defence of Slovenia took part in the killing of unarmed soldiers in considerable numbers? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the actual number, but I do know that there was a certain number of casualties, or rather, killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the barracks were surrounded, that is where soldiers lived; otherwise, there were power cuts. There was shortage of water, and that these barracks were fired at as well?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the information that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to prevent the loss of young lives and casualties in the army ranks, the decision was passed for the army to withdraw, is that right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did all Slovenian officers and soldiers accede to the Territorial Defence and that became the army of Slovenia? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, I do not know about exact figures; but according to the information we had, most of them, yes, most of the officers who were Slovenian crossed over to the Territorial Defence of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence keep most of the weaponry, or by then it was already the army of the Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: That's the information that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was still within the SFRY, is that right, at that time?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Slovenia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA withdraw from Slovenia in different directions through Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by sea and land towards Serbia and Montenegro, or rather, Bosnia-Herzegovina, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Croatia, was there the same kind of situation that took place in Slovenia before that, that barracks were under siege and without electricity and water and that soldiers in these barracks were killed?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Yugoslav People's Army withdraw further on from the Republic of Croatia, too, again in different directions?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence and the army of Croatia as it was at that particular time already, did they take over most of the equipment, weaponry that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: That is the information that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did all officers and all soldiers who were in the JNA and who were ethnic Croats join the army of Croatia in that situation?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the army was forced to withdraw further from Croatia, in different directions? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Part of that army arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The army, the Yugoslav People's Army, as it was withdrawing from Croatia through Bosnia-Herzegovina, too, was it being attacked by the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, these paramilitary units, all the way up to Sarajevo because they were moving in that direction as well?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These paramilitary units from Bosnia-Herzegovina were in the territory of Croatia within the ZNG, and later on they came to Bosnia-Herzegovina as already trained and with battle experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, the Yugoslav People's Army had to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Territorial Defence that was in the territories where Serbs lived and Territorial Defence in the areas primarily populated by Muslims, although, there were not the strict delineations everywhere, did they take over the equipment of the army, and did they keep that within their own weaponry?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the way in which the army of Republika Srpska and the BiH army were formed?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the same principles. The forming of both armies was based on the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was divided along ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did all officers and soldiers, Muslim officers and soldiers, join the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. There were some honourable exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the case also with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the people who composed the Territorial Defence in the places where they lived as a majority, did they also, that means, the Serbian soldiers and officers from Bosnia-Herzegovina, joined VRS?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, on the territorial basis, units were formed what I would call of people's army made up of the population or the residents of one or the other ethnicity. So the same situation prevailed in both communities, but the basis was the Territorial Defence. The war broke out before the VRS army was ever formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, in Sarajevo, but in other Bosnian towns as well, were the barracks also surrounded where JNA soldiers were billeted and that they were under fire, they were killed, that were shot by snipers, that they were deprived of food and electricity, the same situation used to prevail in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not only in the barracks but the highest commands as well, even the army commands were in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did something even more specific happen here, meaning that when the JNA started to withdraw from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this particular part of the JNA that was in BH, while they were leaving their barracks and passing through Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they killed?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the most outstanding example is the pullout of the command of the 2nd army under the auspices of UNPROFOR. It's a well-known story of the massacre on Dobrovoljacka Street. Although everything had a been agreed under the sponsorship or auspices of an UNPROFOR commander, a marching column, not a combat column but a marching column, and convoy of vehicles was cut in two and over 100 men were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to mention other incidents, but let me just mention the withdrawal of the army from Tuzla. You know that in the course of the withdrawal of the JNA several hundred soldiers were killed walking in a column without having any intention of carrying out any operation or action?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: I also know about this column, and I know that there was agreement with the local authorities in Tuzla to provide safe pullout of the army. However, as a result of deceit, the column came under the attack. The men were in vehicles. This was not a combat formation, and they didn't expect that they would have to put up resistance because the agreement had been reached to allow the column to be pulled out in a peaceful and orderly manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also know or you heard that several hundred soldiers were killed, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Around 100, that's the information I have, at least 100. And it's possible that more were killed. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: The weapons that the JNA had in Bosnia-Herzegovina was kept by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that of the VRS. .

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that constituted the basis of armament of all formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So each side had at their disposal all kinds of weapons that belonged to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to put a leading question, but who remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina when we talk about the VRS? Who constituted the VRS, and are you able to tell us what their task was?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: 99 per cent of the population, of the Serbian population, made up the army of Republika Srpska, or rather, the army was made up of 99 per cent of ethnic Serbs. Their task was to protect and defend the people who found themselves in the area of VRS, more specifically in Sarajevo and the area of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which means in the territory controlled by the SRC. Of course, the basic principle for an army to be able to carry out its primary task according to all our rules, and it's only logical, it first needed to create conditions to protect itself, because only if an army can survive will it be able to protect someone else. The strategy of the VRS, particularly that of the SRC, was to maintain and preserve the territory populated by the Serbs in Bosnia and Sarajevo and to ensure as normal every day life as possible. Our strategy was not to capture and occupy the whole of Bosnia, but rather to control only those parts of territories that ethnically belonged to the Serbian people, unlike the other side which claimed the right. And their strategy was to capture the whole of Bosnia, and that was their principal goal. Stemming from that was their -- their decision to pursue offensive actions in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, who were members? Let us put aside the population for the moment. Who were members of the army of Republika Srpska. Those were predominantly local ?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: These were members of these ethnic communities that lived in the territory that was at the time controlled by SRC; in other words, those were the people who had been living there for centuries with their families on their land and in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If there were any officers from Serbia, those were for the most part people who had their own families that had also been living there for centuries?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was the case for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that already at beginning, this was in no way any kind of Serbian Montenegro army but made up exclusively by people who were living in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question is: When the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia imposed sanctions on the VRS, the so-called self-styled "VRS," can we say that in 1994 after the beginning of August when the sanctions were imposed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there was no one else there except for the people who were living there for ages and who were defending that you are homes and their loved ones and their own lives. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: That was the case from the very beginning. However, the conditions were much more complex for both the people to survive and also to provide supplies for the VRS and for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in particular, because its position was extremely complex and its tasks were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dragicevic, let us now move to specifics. From the moment when you took -- assumed your duties on the 22nd of November, 1994, at that time when you took up your position, was this situation that I asked you a little bit a while ago still prevailing? I'm talking about the sanctions imposed by the FRY in indication to those imposed by the international community? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, at that time there were shortages of food and fuel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We can also say that there was insufficient quantity of ammunition and weapons?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that particularly referred to large calibre weapons. We were in a very bad position vis-a-vis that particular type of weapons. We were aware what was coming within the next few months, and we were very weakened. Our position was very weakened as a corps in that respect. Unless we were able to fix something and repair something, the whole capability and capacity of putting up an efficient resistance would come under question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In November 1994, you already knew that units of the BH army were superior both in manpower strength but also in terms of weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were superior in every respect, except in the domain of combat morale and strict military discipline of the corps that was positioned opposite the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and I'm talking about the 1st BH Army Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty; that is to say, from late November 1994, you strictly adhered to the heavy weapon exclusion zone and you never violated it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I do know that from the staff meetings and as a result of inspection of units, that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you also knew that the BH army frequently violated the exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were violations, but I cannot say exactly how many. There's probably is a document to corroborate that, so there were violations of truce by the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived, you knew that from the month of August 1994 and onwards, an offensive and action of the BH army was primarily focussed in the Nisic plateau - and later on I'm going to place before you a map - and also the Trnovski positions? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is where most of the combat took place; that is to say, in two completely different directions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which meant that we were overstretched. Also, there were attacks coming from the part of Sarajevo that was under the command of the 2nd -- under the control of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Well, at the point when this started, we did not know what the main thrust of the attack would be. This was a strategy that was in their view supposed to yield results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that you and the Main Staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps noticed that the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were otherwise stationed in Sarajevo - I'm referring to the 1st Corps - that many of their forces from Sarajevo were taken out of Sarajevo through this tunnel that existed, and that then they operated in Ilijas, Vogosca, Lukavica, and Trnovo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at first, for the most part, was focussed on the part of the town of Sarajevo that was under their control. As the road was opened, under the runway of Sarajevo airport, which with was then under UNPROFOR control, through that tunnel, actually, they managed to get their forces out because it was their assessment that they could achieve much greater success if they were to attack from the external side. Up until then, they were convinced that from the town itself they could not achieve any meaningful results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can you tell me something else.
